title: A net or boosting
objectives: Frame the question of a network against boosting on tabular returns, and say what the evidence suggests.

screens.title: The first question
screens.prose: This lesson takes about fifteen minutes; interview pace is three minutes a question. The case builds on `ensembles` l12 and `research-int` l11. The interviewer says: "Our boosted trees predict next-day returns for 100 stocks. A researcher wants a network. What do you ask first?"
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: What exactly is the target, and which loss scores it?
How much data is there, in rows and in days?
What do the current trees score, against a simple baseline?
How will the two be compared, on which split?
Which deep learning library the desk uses.
options.why: Tools come after the question is framed; they do not change the decision.

options.text: How many layers the network should have.
options.why: Architecture is a detail of the candidate, decided after the comparison is set up.

hints.text: What would you need to decide between the two?
A metric, a baseline, the data and a fair test.
Target and loss, data size, the current score, the comparison.

feedback.correct: Frame the decision before any model.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what you would need to decide.

byKey.layers: Layers are the candidate's detail; first agree how a winner is decided.

explain.text: These four questions turn "should we use a network" into a comparison with a metric. The answers decide the rest of the case.

screens.title: What the evidence says
screens.prose: Grinsztajn, Oyallon and Varoquaux (2022) report that on medium-sized tabular data trees usually win. Here is a simulated panel built to look like that: 100 stocks by 500 days, the last 150 days for testing. Slide between the two seeds.
screens.question: On seed 0, what share of the oracle's $R^2$ does boosting reach? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: The oracle knows the true signal; no model can beat it on average.
Boosting has $0.0386$, the oracle $0.0411$.

feedback.correct: About $0.94$: boosting is close to the best possible.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide boosting's $R^2$ by the oracle's.

byKey.mlp: That is the network's share. Read boosting's bar.

explain.text: Even the oracle explains only $0.0411$ of the variance: daily returns are mostly noise. Boosting reaches about $0.94$ of that ceiling, which leaves a network little room.

screens.title: Frame it as a comparison
screens.prose: Say the frame in one breath before any modelling.
screens.question: Order your framing. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: The target is next-day return, scored by out-of-sample $R^2$ on later days.
The baselines are ridge and the current boosted trees.
The network must beat the trees on the same split, by a paired test across days.
If it does on two seeds, we run it in parallel before switching.
We pick the model with the higher training $R^2$.
lines.why: Training $R^2$ rewards fitting noise; the decision uses later days only.

hints.text: Metric first, then baselines.
Then the test, then what would change the decision.
Target and metric, baselines, the test, the condition.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build from the metric to the decision.

byKey.fx: Training scores reward noise-fitting; use later days.

explain.text: The frame fixes what "better" means before anyone sees a result. That is what makes the later comparison believable.

screens.title: Name the baseline
screens.prose: A model is only as good as what it beats. Read seed 0.
screens.question: How much $R^2$ do the trees add over ridge on seed 0? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Subtract ridge's bar from boosting's.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract ridge from boosting.

byKey.mlp: That is the network's gain over ridge.
byKey.sign: Boosting is above ridge, so the gain is positive.

explain.text: The trees add $0.0155$ over ridge, and the network $0.0051$. Gains this size are normal in returns, so the test must be sensitive.

screens.title: What would change the decision
screens.prose: State in advance what result would make you switch.
screens.question: Which condition do you state?

options.text: The network beats the trees in a paired test over test days, with $|t| > 2$, on two seeds.
The network's $R^2$ is higher on one split.
options.why: One split can rank two close models either way by chance.

options.text: The network has a lower training loss than the trees.
options.why: Training loss rewards fitting noise; it says nothing about later days.

options.text: The network is at least ten times larger.
options.why: Size is not evidence; the comparison on later days is.

hints.text: A single number cannot separate two close models.
Use the paired differences across days.
Name the test and the number of seeds in advance.

feedback.correct: A pre-stated test, on more than one seed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What result would convince a sceptic?

byKey.any: One split is one draw; state a test.

explain.text: Stating the bar before the result stops anyone moving it afterwards. l10 builds the test.

screens.title: More powerful, so it wins?
screens.prose: A candidate says: "Networks are universal approximators, so the network will beat the trees with enough tuning."
screens.question: What is the right reply?

options.text: Capacity is not the issue; with noisy, irregular tabular data the trees' inductive bias often wins.
Agree: tuning will close the gap.
options.why: On this panel the network trails by $0.0104$ of $R^2$, and more tuning chases noise.

options.text: Networks never work on tabular data.
options.why: They can win when the signal is smooth and oblique; l11 builds such a panel.

hints.text: Could a network represent the trees' function? Yes. Does it learn it from noisy data?
Learning depends on the bias of the method and the data, not on capacity.
Trees cut on single features, which suits thresholds and useless features.

feedback.correct: Inductive bias, not capacity, decides on noisy tabular data.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Separate what a model can represent from what it learns from noisy data.

byKey.agree: Tuning a flexible model on noisy data mostly fits more noise.

explain.text: Universal approximation says the function exists, not that training finds it from a few per cent of signal. Grinsztajn et al. find trees win on irregular targets with uninformative features.

screens.title: A small dataset
screens.prose: The researcher has only 20 stocks by 200 days: 2,800 training rows. The same three models on a smooth-signal panel give these test $R^2$: boosting $-0.029$, network $0.0236$, ridge $0.0222$.
screens.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: With 2,800 noisy rows, 200 boosting rounds overfit; size the model to the data.
Networks are better on small data.
options.why: Ridge does as well as the network here: it is regularisation that wins, not the network.

options.text: A negative $R^2$ means a bug.
options.why: Out of sample, a model worse than the test mean has negative $R^2$; it is overfitting, not a bug.

hints.text: What does a negative out-of-sample $R^2$ mean?
Worse than predicting the test mean.
Boosting fitted the noise in 2,800 rows.

feedback.correct: Small data punishes a large model; regularise or shrink it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read what a negative test $R^2$ means.

explain.text: Out of sample, $R^2$ is negative when a model does worse than the test mean. On small panels shrink the trees (fewer rounds, early stopping) before concluding anything about networks.

screens.title: It depends on the data's shape
screens.prose: The spoken answer: which model wins depends on the shape of the signal, the data size and the noise, so we test it. $$\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{net}} - R^2_{\text{trees}}, \text{ judged by a paired test over days}$$
screens.question: Which panel would favour the network?

options.text: A smooth signal along a combination of all eight features.
A signal that jumps when one feature crosses a level.
options.why: Trees cut on one feature at a time, which fits a jump exactly.

options.text: Six of eight features pure noise.
options.why: Trees ignore useless features more easily than a network.

feedback.correct: Smooth and oblique favours the network.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how a tree splits.

explain.text: A tree approximates a diagonal, smooth surface with many small steps; a network fits it directly. l11 builds exactly that panel.

screens.title: A model change at a fund
screens.prose: At a fund, swapping the production return model moves real money. The researcher has already tried twenty network variants on the test period.
screens.question: What do you insist on before the comparison?

options.text: A fresh test period, with the metric, test and seeds written down in advance.
Report the best of the twenty variants on the same period.
options.why: Picking the best of twenty on the test period overstates it.

options.text: Nothing; the researcher is experienced.
options.why: Experience does not remove the selection effect of twenty tries.

hints.text: What happens when you pick the best of twenty on one period?
Its score is biased upwards.
Hold out new data and fix the rules first.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about choosing the best of twenty.

byKey.best: The best of twenty is lucky by construction.

explain.text: Twenty tries on one period make the best one look better than it is. A fresh period and rules fixed in advance remove that bias.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests. Three are hand cases for `r2_out_of_sample`, one with a mean of 12 and one worse than the mean. Then a hand case for `r2_from_days`, and the file's world A seed 0 rounded to 4 places, then its ordering. Numbers are compared to $10^{-9}$ relative.

mutants.symptom: Divides by the sum of squares about 0, not about the mean.
Returns the error share, forgetting the 1 minus.
Averages a daily R^2 instead of summing errors and variances first.

hints.text: $R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$, with SST about the mean of $y$.
Each day has the same number of stocks, so day sums give the same ratio.
`1 - sum(mse) / sum(var_y)`.

feedback.generic: Not yet. Check the denominator and the 1 minus.

byKey.test-1: The first hand case is off: $1 - 0.75/5 = 0.85$. Return one minus the error share, with the total sum of squares about the mean of $y$, not about 0.
byKey.test-4: The day version is off. Sum the errors and the variances first, then divide once.

explain.text: Out of sample, $R^2$ can be negative: a model worse than the test mean. Summing day errors and day variances gives exactly `r2_score` because every day has 100 stocks.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer goes on: "What would make you say yes?"
screens.question: Which answer do you give?

options.text: A paired win over days on fresh data and two seeds, an interval clear of 0, and a gain that survives costs.
A higher $R^2$ than the trees on the test period.
options.why: One period is one draw, and $R^2$ ignores costs and turnover.

options.text: A higher backtest Sharpe ratio than the trees.
options.why: Useful, but it needs the same paired test and costs as well.

hints.text: Combine the frame and the test.
Fresh data, paired test, more than one seed.
And it must still pay after costs.

feedback.correct: Evidence, an interval, and P&L after costs.
feedback.generic: Not quite. One number on one period is not enough.

explain.text: The yes is conditional and stated up front: a paired win with an interval clear of 0, on fresh data, that still pays after costs.

ideas: Frame "net or boosting" as a comparison: target and loss, data size, baselines, and a pre-stated test.
On medium-sized, noisy tabular data trees usually win; here boosting reaches $0.0386$ against an oracle of $0.0411$.
Small data punishes a large model: size the trees to the data before concluding anything about networks.

formula.name: Out-of-sample R²
formula.note: Negative when a model does worse than the test mean.

summary.trap: "Networks are more powerful, so they win" confuses capacity with what a model learns from noisy data.

quiz.question: A model's test-set squared errors sum to 1,050; the target's squared deviations from the test mean sum to 1,000. What is its out-of-sample $R^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. One minus SSE over SST.

byKey.sign: It is worse than the mean, so negative.
byKey.ratio: That is SSE over SST; subtract it from 1.

explain.text: The model does worse than predicting the test mean, so $R^2 = 1 - 1.05 = -0.05$.

quiz.question: Which property of tabular data, reported by Grinsztajn et al., favours trees?

options.text: Many features carry no information about the target.
Very large datasets of many millions of rows.
options.why: Large data helps networks most; the finding is for medium-sized data.

options.text: Smooth targets along combinations of features.
options.why: That favours networks, which are not tied to single-feature splits.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which property makes single-feature splits strong?

explain.text: Trees choose one informative feature per split and ignore the rest; networks spread weight across every input.

quiz.question: The oracle's test $R^2$ is $0.0369$ and boosting's is $0.0342$. What gain is left for any model? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract boosting from the oracle.

byKey.share: That is the share reached, not the gap.

explain.text: Only $0.0027$ of $R^2$ separates boosting from the best possible model on average. A network can gain at most that.
